claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (co-founder of Bloom Nutrition) defines luck as the product of actions taken to place yourself in environments where opportunities arise: luck is not random but is controlled by deliberate environment selection. The mechanism is that high-opportunity environments present options that are simply unavailable in low-opportunity environments; choosing the environment is choosing the opportunity set.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: requires active and intentional environment selection, not passive presence
claims.mechanism: High-opportunity environments expose participants to deals, relationships, and referrals that do not exist in their default environment; environment selection is the upstream input that determines the opportunity distribution you draw from.
bounded_by: Does not account for within-environment conversion rates (being in the room is necessary but not sufficient)

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia (co-founder of Bloom Nutrition, Aspen networking trip, 2024) asserts that being in a room with people who are doing bigger things than you expands your perception of what your own business is capable of and how much bigger it could be. The mechanism is perceptual recalibration: observing peers operating at a higher scale updates your internal reference point for what is achievable with your current assets.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: requires in-person, real-time exposure to higher-performing peers (not just reading about them)
most impactful when the peer's business model or market is adjacent to your own
claims.mechanism: Firsthand exposure to operators achieving larger outcomes with comparable inputs recalibrates the internal benchmark for what is possible; the upward reference shift translates into bolder strategic decisions immediately after the interaction.
bounded_by: Effect is described as felt in real life vs. reading or watching; remote or asynchronous exposure may not produce the same perceptual shift

examples.text: At a networking event in Aspen during a Platform Office (a CPG-focused brokerage) visit, Greg LaVecchia found himself in a room with founders and executives from the largest consumer packaged goods brands. Leaving that room, he described being fired up and thinking significantly bigger about what his own Glacier Crush brand could achieve. The example illustrates how peer-group recalibration occurs in real time: the room contained operators building at a scale LaVecchia had not yet reached, and the conversation directly shifted his ambition ceiling upward within a single conversation.

An unnamed founder of Frozen One Protein (a 40g-protein ice cream brand launched into Wegmans nationwide, Central Market, Bristol Farms, and confirmed for Target) described growing from near-zero followers to 36,000 followers and 10 million video views from a single before-and-after acne transformation post. The video contained no narrative explanation of how the transformation happened; the visual contrast alone was enough to generate the audience response. He described it as: there is nothing more instantly recognizable than a transformation. The example illustrates that in short-form content, before/after visual proof requires no story or explanation to convert attention into followers.

practices.text: Deliberately invest in physical presence in locations (e.g., property, memberships, event attendance) where high-caliber entrepreneurs and operators regularly congregate across multiple seasons of the year, not only at scheduled industry events.

Prioritize in-person networking trips and events even when short (24 hours) over skipping them due to schedule constraints; the opportunity density of high-quality peer rooms is not replicable remotely.
